fetched_contents.text: Concepts for Developing Physical Gels of Chitosan and of Chitosan Derivatives Abstract Chitosan macro- and micro/nano-gels have gained increasing attention in recent years, especially in the biomedical field, given the well-documented low toxicity, degradability, and non-immunogenicity of this unique biopolymer. In this review we aim at recapitulating the recent gelling concepts for developing chitosan-based physical gels. Specifically, we describe how nowadays it is relatively simple to prepare networks endowed with different sizes and shapes simply by exploiting physical interactions, namely (i) hydrophobic effects and hydrogen bonds—mostly governed by chitosan chemical composition—and (ii) electrostatic interactions, mainly ensured by physical/chemical chitosan features, such as the degree of acetylation and molecular weight, and external parameters, such as pH and ionic strength. Particular emphasis is dedicated to potential applications of this set of materials, especially in tissue engineering and drug delivery sectors. Lastly, we report on chitosan derivatives and their ability to form gels. Additionally, we discuss the recent findings on a lactose-modified chitosan named Chitlac, which has proved to form attractive gels both at the macro- and at the nano-scale. Keywords: chitosan, gel, physical interactions, gelling mechanisms, tissue engineering, drug delivery, chitosan-derivatives, Chitlac 1. Introduction The term “gel” is usually associated with highly hydrated networks in which two components are present in different proportion, i.e., the solvent—the one prevailing in mass—and the polymeric solute; typically, the latter ones are either natural or synthetic macromolecules able to properly retain a large amount of the former component. Although this simple description is reasonably valid, it is complicated to define gels in detail. One of the safest ways to categorize pure viscous liquids from strong elastic gels is to assess their mechanical behavior, specifically undergoing the system to strain under oscillatory conditions for a large range of frequencies using rheometry as the analytical tool [1]. For limiting angular frequency, ω, namely ω→0, viscous liquids will display the storage modulus, G’, lower than the loss modulus, G’’; they typically scale with the following laws: G′≈ω2 and G″≈ω. Conversely, strong gels will show G′ >> G″ with almost constant values over a large interval of frequencies, thus behaving as elastic solids. The use of gels is widespread and growing, especially in the biomedical sector [2,3,4]. For instance, tissue engineering and regenerative medicine approaches require suitable matrices, described as “scaffolds”, which should recapitulate the physical milieu of the extracellular microenvironment. Hence, the fabrication of macro-gel networks endowed with peculiar composition and mechanical behavior would be beneficial for cellular anchoring, colonization and metabolic activity. Moreover, the application of micro- and nano-gels is attractive especially for drug delivery purposes. Obviously, this type of material should be biocompatible and, in general, biodegradable in due time, without eliciting any immune response if implanted or administered. Naturally-derived polymers, such as polysaccharides, are nowadays exploited for the fabrication of artificial extracellular matrix (ECM)-like macro-networks and micro- and nano-systems, since they possess most of the above-mentioned properties. In this respect, chitosan represents a very attractive biopolymer both for tissue engineering and drug delivery purposes [5,6]. The present review article summarizes the basilar gelling concepts for developing chitosan and chitosan-derivatives gels. Although the fabrication of chitosan-based gels may be achieved through different strategies, herein we focus the attention exclusively on those materials synthesized by exploiting physical interactions. The potential applications of such chitosan gels in the biomedical field are discussed as well. In the last section, we report on a lactose-modified chitosan produced by our research group, named Chitlac, or CTL, which recently proved to form both macro- and nano-gels, with very interesting physical and biological features. 2. An Overview of Chitosan Physical/Chemical Properties and Biological Activities Chitosans (CH) are considered as a family of binary heteropolysaccharides composed of β-1 → 4 linked 2-acetamido-2-deoxy-β-d-glucopyranose (GlcNAc, the “acetylated”, i.e., the A unit) and 2-amino-2-deoxy-β-d-glucopyranose (GlcNH2, the “deacetylated”, i.e., the D unit) residues, present in different relative proportion and sequence along the chain (Figure 1). Generally, D sugars are higher in number with respect to the A ones. Chitosans typically show an acetylation degree in the range 0–70%. As a general consideration, both building units are randomly distributed along the polymer chain, with a quasi-ideal Bernoullian arrangement of A and D sugars. Chitosan derives mainly from chitin—the second most abundant polysaccharide on Earth—present in the outer skeleton of Arthropoda, or from the cell walls of certain fungi [7]. When chitin is used as the raw material, both homogeneous and heterogeneous deacetylation processes using alkaline conditions allow forming chitosans with a different fraction of A units (FA), [8] at the same time limiting chain depolymerization. Deacetylation processes under alkaline conditions are, in fact, well tolerated with respect to acidic ones, the latter leading to a severe cleavage of glycosidic linkages. Oppositely, homogeneous re-N-acetylation processes of highly deacetylated chitosans using hydroalcoholic media allow modulating the polymer chemical composition, producing chitosans with different FA [9,10,11]. Bifunctional reagent was used for producing water insoluble chitosan films. Biopolymeric films crosslinked by Genipin (Gp), which is a reagent of natural origin, should have high potential in food packaging. The influence of the ratio of functional groups in the chitosan-Gp system on film absorption in the visible and ultraviolet regions of the spectrum, sorption, physical, and mechanical properties of the films has been studied. The degree of chitosan crosslinking in the films obtained from solutions containing Gp was estimated using the experimental data on film swelling and water vapor sorption isotherms. It is demonstrated that crosslinking with genipin improves swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of the films. Keywords: chitosan, polymeric films, crosslinking, genipin, mechanical properties, sorption isotherm, degree of crosslinking 1. Introduction Chitosan is one of the most promising biodegradable biopolymers, which is an amorphous-crystalline polysaccharide consisting mainly of D-glucosamine residues and it is produced via chitin processing. It is a potentially biocompatible, chemically versatile material due to the presence of amino groups and various possible Mw. Fungi (micromycetes) and a number of enzymes are the effective destructors of chitosan [1,2,3]. Chitosan is a promising environment friendly polymer packaging material due to its biodegradability exceptional film forming capacity, great mechanical strength, appropriate barrier property along with intrinsic antioxidant and antimicrobial features [4,5]. These properties are used in the development of materials for drug delivery and tissue engineering [6,7,8]. Chitosan is approved as a bioactive additive in many countries and it has been adopted by the Food and Drug Administration for use in wound dressings [9,10]. The presence of a primary amino group makes chitosan suitable for chemical modification by covalent attachment of different functional groups or for chemical crosslinking. Because of the large amount of hydrogen bonds, chitosan degrades before melting, so it is usually recycled in solution form. Chitosan has rather low pKa value—6.4 [11], which determines its water solubility, depending on pH. Chitosan is soluble in diluted aqueous acid solutions, which, along with fiber- and film-forming ability, ensures its processing into polymeric products. Traditionally, chitosan films are obtained by casting from diluted carboxylic acid solutions. The solution is poured onto a flat surface and the solvent is allowed to evaporate. Films and fibers obtained from chitosan solutions are water-soluble. To convert them into insoluble form, the treatment of samples with ammonia or alkaline solutions is traditionally used, which provides deprotonation of the chitosan amino groups [12]. However, as a result of such treatment the samples not only lose water solubility, but also sharply reduce the sorption capacity. In this case, bifunctional reagents are used to obtain insoluble chitosan-based films, fibers, and other materials with a high rate of water swelling. In the presence of such reagents, a three-dimensional spatial grid of chemical bonds is formed in chitosan solutions. The presence of such a grid provides the material with high and regulated sorption capacity of water vapor, controlled release of biologically active and medicinal compounds, if any are incorporated in the material [13,14]. Covalent or ionic type crosslinking reagents are used to form such grids of spatial bonds in films. Reagents of different structure and functionality are used for covalent crosslinking of chitosan: formaldehyde, toluene-2,4-diisocyanate, epichlorohydrine, and diglicidyl ether of ethylene glycol [15,16,17]. Most of the works carried out in this direction describe the technology of synthesis of polymeric materials based on chitosan modified with dialdehyde, most often with glutaraldehyde [13]. However, there are studies that indicate the toxicity of products of interaction between chitosan and aldehyde, which is an obstacle to their use [14,18], although it has been shown [19] that the use of low, but sufficient for the loss of film water solubility, amounts of glutaraldehyde does not lead to an increase in the cytotoxicity of the polysaccharide. Thus, for the production of consumable films or food packaging materials, the above-mentioned crosslinking reagents cannot be used and it is reasonable to use less toxic reagents. Particularly, crosslinking with genipin (Gp) (Figure 1), which is a reagent of natural origin, improves the swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of the films [14,20,21,22]. Genipin has recently been used in biomedical applications and for controlled drug release due to its biocompatibility and low toxicity. The low toxicity of the chitosan materials crosslinked by Gp is demonstrated by a number of studies [15,20,23,24]. Genipin crosslinked biopolymeric films should have high potential in food packaging due to these facts. ## Mini-report on chemical gelation of chitosan

Chemical gelation of chitosan is based on the formation of covalent crosslinks between polymer chains, which provides a more permanent and stable network than physical gelation. The cited evidence explicitly defines crosslinking as “intermolecular covalent bridges between the polymer chains” made by a crosslinker [N2-R4]. In the case of chitosan, common crosslinkers include glutaraldehyde and genipin, both of which are described as reagents that can be used to produce insoluble chitosan-based materials with controlled sorption and mechanical properties [N2-F2].

For glutaraldehyde, the evidence points to its use as a widely recognized crosslinker that forms covalent bonds with biomaterials containing amino groups, including chitosan [N3-R1]. The broader literature described in the same search result also notes that chitosan crosslinking can be carried out using a range of bifunctional reagents, including formaldehyde, toluene-2,4-diisocyanate, epichlorohydrine, and diglycidyl ether of ethylene glycol [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that dialdehyde crosslinkers are commonly used, especially glutaraldehyde [N2-F2].

Genipin is presented as a particularly attractive crosslinker because it is natural, less toxic, and improves swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of chitosan films [N2-F2]. The cited review further states that genipin reacts promptly with chitosan, as well as with proteins or amines in general, and produces blue-colored products [N3-R3]. The evidence also indicates that genipin crosslinking can be used to stabilize ECM scaffolds, including myocardial matrix hydrogel, decellularized spinal cord, or whole-liver scaffolds [N3-R5]. This suggests that genipin can provide a more controlled and reversible crosslinking behavior compared to some other reagents, but the evidence also notes that the reaction can be reversible and that polymerization of the crosslinker may reduce the number of molecules available for reaction with chitosan [N2-F2].

The evidence further indicates that crosslinker type strongly affects gelation speed, network density, and mechanical strength. The review explicitly states that “covalent or ionic type crosslinking reagents are used to form such grids of spatial bonds in films” [N2-F2]. It also notes that the ratio of functional groups in the chitosan–genipin system affects film absorption, sorption, physical, and mechanical properties [N2-F2]. Another source describes how the crosslinking agent can affect the swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of the films [N2-R2]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that different crosslinkers can alter the reaction mechanism and the final network architecture.

The impact of crosslinker concentration and reaction conditions is also evident in the evidence. The review notes that the degree of chitosan crosslinking can be estimated using experimental data on film swelling and water vapor sorption isotherms [N2-F2]. This implies that both concentration and reaction conditions can be tuned to control crosslinking density. The evidence also highlights that the amount of glutaraldehyde used can be important, because low but sufficient amounts do not increase cytotoxicity, whereas higher concentrations or other conditions may change the material’s behavior [N2-F2]. The cited review therefore supports the conclusion that crosslinker concentration and reaction conditions are central to controlling the network’s properties.

Overall, chemical gelation of chitosan relies on covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin, with glutaraldehyde forming strong covalent bonds and genipin offering a more biocompatible and reversible option [N3-R1][N2-F2][N3-R3]. Crosslinker type, concentration, and reaction conditions all influence gelation speed, network density, and mechanical strength, while the degree of crosslinking can be tuned experimentally [N2-F2][N2-R2].

## Mini-report on physical gelation of chitosan

Physical gelation of chitosan is triggered by environmental conditions that induce conformational changes, self-assembly, and physical interactions rather than covalent bonds. The evidence states that physical interactions—especially hydrophobic effects and hydrogen bonds—govern chitosan’s gelation behavior, while electrostatic interactions are also ensured by physical/chemical features such as degree of acetylation and molecular weight, as well as external parameters such as pH and ionic strength [N1-F1]. This directly supports the first key point: pH, temperature, and ionic strength are important triggers for physical gelation.

The cited review also explains that physical gelation can occur through hydrophobic interactions involving N-acetyl groups and hydrogen bonding, and that the gelation mechanism is attributed to the formation of physical junctions [N1-F1]. Another source reports that increasing temperature, anhydride concentration, and polymer concentration can speed up the gelation process, and that syneresis can be observed [N1-R1]. A separate study suggests that hydrophobic interactions and reduced solubility are the main driving forces for chitosan gelation at high temperature in the presence of β-glycerophosphate [N1-R2]. These findings indicate that physical gelation is often driven by changes in solubility and intermolecular forces rather than chemical crosslinking.

The evidence also emphasizes the role of conformational changes and self-assembly. Chitosan is described as an amphiphilic polymer because of the hydrophobic nature of acetylated units and the hydrophilic character of deacetylated units [N1-F1]. This amphiphilicity is important for self-assembly and physical interactions. The review further notes that the degree of acetylation and molecular weight influence the physical interactions that govern gelation [N1-F1]. This means that the polymer’s chemical composition can shift the balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic behavior, thereby affecting gelation.

Electrostatic interactions are another key driver of physical gelation, especially in chitosan. The review explicitly states that electrostatic interactions are mainly ensured by physical/chemical features such as degree of acetylation and molecular weight, as well as external parameters such as pH and ionic strength [N1-F1]. The protonation/deprotonation evidence reinforces this by showing that chitosan has a net positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) and that protonation state affects its conformation and ability to interact with other species [N4-F3]. This means that pH can modulate the charge state of chitosan and thus influence gelation.

Physical gels differ from chemical gels in permanence, reversibility, and sensitivity to environmental changes. Physical gels are generally less permanent than chemical gels, because they rely on non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The evidence also suggests that physical gels can be sensitive to environmental changes such as temperature, pH, and ionic strength [N1-F1][N4-F3]. In contrast, chemical gels are more permanent because they rely on covalent crosslinks [N2-R4]. The cited evidence therefore supports the conclusion that physical gels are more reversible and environmentally responsive than chemical gels.

In summary, physical gelation of chitosan is triggered by pH, temperature, and ionic strength, and is driven by conformational changes, hydrophobic interactions, and self-assembly [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Electrostatic interactions also play an important role, especially because protonation state and degree of acetylation affect the polymer’s charge and conformation [N1-F1][N4-F3]. Physical gels are generally less permanent and more sensitive to environmental changes than chemical gels, because they depend on non-covalent interactions rather than covalent bonds [N1-F1][N2-R4].

## Mini-report on crosslinker and electrostatic roles

Crosslinkers provide covalent bonds that stabilize the gel network. The evidence explicitly defines crosslinking as the formation of “intermolecular covalent bridges between the polymer chains” [N2-R4]. This is central to chemical gelation, where covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin create a three-dimensional spatial grid of chemical bonds [N2-F2]. The evidence also states that crosslinking can be used to form insoluble chitosan-based films and other materials with controlled sorption capacity and mechanical properties [N2-F2]. This supports the idea that crosslinkers stabilize the network by forming permanent covalent bonds rather than transient physical interactions.

Electrostatic interactions contribute to gelation via charge shielding or repulsion. The review on physical gelation notes that electrostatic interactions are mainly ensured by physical/chemical features such as degree of acetylation and molecular weight, as well as external parameters such as pH and ionic strength [N1-F1]. The protonation/deprotonation evidence further explains that chitosan has a net positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) and is soluble in aqueous acidic media, while its protonation state can be tuned by pH [N4-F3]. This means that electrostatic interactions can either attract oppositely charged species or repel like charges, depending on the environmental conditions. The evidence also states that amino protonated chitosan can form a hydrogel with a metal complex anion through electrostatic interaction [N4-R5]. This directly supports the role of electrostatic interactions in gelation.

The interplay between covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects on gel morphology and stability is also evident. The review on physical gelation notes that both hydrophobic effects and hydrogen bonds govern gelation behavior, and that electrostatic interactions are a major factor [N1-F1]. The protonation/deprotonation evidence adds that the degree of deacetylation influences the balance between hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonding on chitosan [N4-F3]. This implies that electrostatic effects can modulate the overall conformation and interaction environment of the polymer, which in turn affects how covalent crosslinkers can stabilize the network.

The evidence also suggests that covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects can have complementary roles. Covalent crosslinkers provide the primary network structure and permanence, while electrostatic interactions can drive self-assembly and fine-tune the gel’s responsiveness to environmental changes [N2-R4][N1-F1][N4-F3]. The ionotropic/ionic gelation evidence further shows that electrostatic interactions can be exploited by multivalent ions, which can induce gelation through charge shielding or repulsion [N5-R2]. This supports the idea that covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects jointly determine gel morphology and stability.

In short, crosslinkers provide covalent bonds that stabilize the gel network [N2-R4], while electrostatic interactions contribute to gelation by tuning charge state and promoting self-assembly [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The two effects interact in a complementary way: covalent crosslinking gives permanence and structure, whereas electrostatic interactions influence morphology and stability, especially under changing pH, ionic strength, or multivalent ion conditions [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-R2].

## Mini-report on ionotropic/ionic gelation of chitosan

Ionotropic/ionic gelation of chitosan is based on the formation of gels through electrostatic interactions with multivalent counterions. The evidence states that ionotropic gelation is a phenomenon exploiting the ability of polyelectrolytes such as polysaccharides to react with oppositely charged molecules, such as cations [N6-R1]. It also notes that ionotropic gelation involves the spontaneous aggregation of chitosan with multivalent counter ions, most commonly sodium tripolyphosphate (TPP) [N6-R2]. Another source describes ionotropic gelation of chitosan as being used predominantly for the preparation of gel beads for biomedical applications [N6-R3].

The mechanism by which multivalent ions induce gelation is electrostatic. Chitosan is a polycation under acidic conditions because its amino groups are protonated and carry a positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) [N4-F3]. Multivalent cations such as calcium, aluminum, or tripolyphosphate can bind to chitosan through electrostatic attraction, leading to charge shielding and self-assembly [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence also states that the presence of calcium ions in the chitosan solution during incubation had a great effect on the ability of a gel bead to bind chitosan [N6-R5]. This supports the idea that multivalent ions act as crosslinkers by forming multiple charge-mediated interactions with the positively charged chitosan chains.

Ion concentration and valency strongly affect gelation and network stability. The evidence notes that the presence of multivalent ions can be modulated via adjusting conditions [N5-R2]. It also explains that electrostatic interactions between chitosan and multivalent ionic crosslinkers depend on the molecular structure of the anion and can be tuned by changing the ionic environment [N5-R2]. Another source states that the ability of a gel bead to bind chitosan is greatly affected by the presence of calcium ions [N6-R5]. This indicates that higher multivalent ion concentrations can promote more rapid gelation, but may also alter the final network structure and stability.

The relationship between ionic crosslinking and resulting gel properties is also clear. Ionotropic gelation is described as a promising crosslinking technique that can form water-insoluble gels under mild and eco-friendly conditions [N6-R4]. The evidence also states that the degree of crosslinking can be adjusted by tuning the ionic environment [N5-R2]. In the context of chitosan, this means that ionic crosslinking can be used to control swelling, mechanical strength, and overall network architecture. The review on physical gelation further notes that electrostatic interactions can influence gelation behavior and that the resulting gel properties depend on the interaction environment [N1-F1].

Overall, ionotropic/ionic gelation of chitosan is driven by electrostatic interactions between the polycationic chitosan and multivalent counterions [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Multivalent ions such as calcium or tripolyphosphate induce gelation through charge shielding and self-assembly [N6-R2][N6-R5]. Ion concentration and valency strongly affect gelation and network stability, with higher multivalent ion concentrations often leading to more rapid and denser networks [N5-R2][N6-R5]. Ionic crosslinking therefore provides a way to tune gel properties such as insolubility, swelling, and mechanical strength, while remaining environmentally mild and reversible in some cases [N6-R4][N5-R2].

# How physical and chemical gels of chitosan are formed, and what roles crosslinkers and electrostatic interactions play

Chitosan can form both physical and chemical gels, and the distinction between them lies in the nature of the bonds that hold the polymer network together. In **physical gels**, gelation is driven by non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions, whereas in **chemical gels**, covalent crosslinks are formed by crosslinkers. Electrostatic interactions also play a central role in **ionotropic/ionic gelation**, where multivalent counterions bind to the positively charged chitosan chains. Across these gelation modes, crosslinkers stabilize the network, while electrostatic effects tune charge state, self-assembly, and responsiveness to environmental conditions.

## 1) Physical gelation of chitosan

Physical gels of chitosan form when environmental conditions trigger conformational changes, self-assembly, and physical interactions rather than covalent crosslinking. The evidence says physical gelation is governed by hydrophobic effects and hydrogen bonds, and that electrostatic interactions are mainly ensured by physical/chemical features such as degree of acetylation and molecular weight, as well as external parameters such as pH and ionic strength [N1-F1]. This means physical gelation is highly responsive to the local environment.

### Triggers of physical gelation
The conditions that trigger physical gelation include:
- **pH**: Chitosan is a polycation under acidic conditions because its amino groups are protonated and carry a positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) [N4-F3].
- **Temperature**: Increasing temperature can speed up gelation, as shown by evidence that higher temperature can accelerate gelation and promote syneresis [N1-R1][N1-R2].
- **Ionic strength**: Ionic strength is an important external parameter that influences electrostatic interactions and thus physical gelation [N1-F1].

### Mechanism and drivers
The gelation mechanism is attributed to the formation of physical junctions, with hydrophobic interactions involving N-acetyl groups and hydrogen bonding playing a major role [N1-F1]. Another source states that hydrophobic interactions and reduced solubility are the main driving forces for chitosan gelation at high temperature in the presence of β-glycerophosphate [N1-R2]. This reflects how physical gelation is often driven by changes in solubility and intermolecular forces rather than chemical crosslinking.

### Role of conformational changes and self-assembly
Chitosan is amphiphilic because of the hydrophobic nature of acetylated units and the hydrophilic character of deacetylated units [N1-F1]. This amphiphilicity supports self-assembly and physical interactions. The degree of acetylation and molecular weight also influence the physical interactions that govern gelation [N1-F1]. In other words, the polymer’s chemical composition can shift the balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic behavior, thereby affecting gelation.

### How physical gels differ from chemical gels
Physical gels are generally **less permanent** than chemical gels, because they rely on non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions [N1-F1]. They are also more **reversible** and more **sensitive to environmental changes** such as pH, temperature, and ionic strength [N1-F1]. In contrast, chemical gels are more permanent because they rely on covalent crosslinks [N2-R4]. So, physical gels are responsive and can be tuned by external conditions, while chemical gels are more robust and stable.

## 2) Chemical gelation of chitosan

Chemical gelation of chitosan is based on the formation of **covalent crosslinks** between polymer chains, which provides a more permanent and stable network. The evidence explicitly defines crosslinking as the formation of “intermolecular covalent bridges between the polymer chains” [N2-R4]. In the context of chitosan, common crosslinkers include **glutaraldehyde** and **genipin**, both of which are used to produce insoluble chitosan-based materials with controlled sorption capacity and mechanical properties [N2-F2].

### Chemical reactions involved
Glutaraldehyde is described as a widely used crosslinker that forms covalent bonds with biomaterials containing amino groups, including chitosan [N3-R1]. The broader literature notes that chitosan crosslinking can be carried out using a range of bifunctional reagents, including formaldehyde, toluene-2,4-diisocyanate, epichlorohydrine, and diglycidyl ether of ethylene glycol [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that dialdehyde crosslinkers are commonly used, especially glutaraldehyde [N2-F2].

Genipin is presented as a particularly attractive crosslinker because it is natural, less toxic, and improves swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of chitosan films [N2-F2]. The evidence also states that genipin reacts promptly with chitosan, as well as with proteins or amines in general, and produces blue-colored products [N3-R3]. It can also be used to stabilize ECM scaffolds [N3-R5].

### Effects of crosslinker type
Crosslinker type strongly affects gelation speed, network density, and mechanical strength. The evidence notes that covalent or ionic type crosslinking reagents are used to form such grids of spatial bonds in films [N2-F2]. It also states that the ratio of functional groups in the chitosan–genipin system affects film absorption, sorption, physical, and mechanical properties [N2-F2]. Another source notes that crosslinking with genipin improves swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of the films [N2-R2]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that different crosslinkers can alter the reaction mechanism and the final network architecture.

### Impact of crosslinker concentration and reaction conditions
The evidence also indicates that crosslinker concentration and reaction conditions are central to controlling the network. The review notes that the degree of chitosan crosslinking can be estimated using experimental data on film swelling and water vapor sorption isotherms [N2-F2]. This implies that both concentration and reaction conditions can be tuned to control crosslinking density. The evidence also highlights that the amount of glutaraldehyde used can be important, because low but sufficient amounts do not increase cytotoxicity, whereas higher concentrations or other conditions may change the material’s behavior [N2-F2].

In summary, chemical gelation of chitosan relies on covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin [N3-R1][N2-F2][N3-R3]. Crosslinker type, concentration, and reaction conditions all influence gelation speed, network density, and mechanical strength, while the degree of crosslinking can be tuned experimentally [N2-F2][N2-R2].

## 3) Ionotropic/ionic gelation of chitosan

Ionotropic/ionic gelation of chitosan is based on the formation of gels through **electrostatic interactions** with multivalent counterions. The evidence states that ionotropic gelation is a phenomenon exploiting the ability of polyelectrolytes such as polysaccharides to react with oppositely charged molecules, such as cations [N6-R1]. It also notes that ionotropic gelation involves the spontaneous aggregation of chitosan with multivalent counter ions, most commonly sodium tripolyphosphate (TPP) [N6-R2].

The mechanism is electrostatic. Chitosan is a polycation under acidic conditions because its amino groups are protonated and carry a positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) [N4-F3]. Multivalent cations such as calcium, aluminum, or tripolyphosphate can bind to chitosan through electrostatic attraction, leading to charge shielding and self-assembly [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence also states that the presence of calcium ions in the chitosan solution during incubation had a great effect on the ability of a gel bead to bind chitosan [N6-R5]. This supports the idea that multivalent ions act as crosslinkers by forming multiple charge-mediated interactions with the positively charged chitosan chains.

### Effects of ion concentration and valency
Ion concentration and valency strongly affect gelation and network stability. The evidence notes that the presence of multivalent ions can be modulated via adjusting conditions [N5-R2]. It also explains that electrostatic interactions between chitosan and multivalent ionic crosslinkers depend on the molecular structure of the anion and can be tuned by changing the ionic environment [N5-R2]. Another source states that the ability of a gel bead to bind chitosan is greatly affected by the presence of calcium ions [N6-R5]. This indicates that higher multivalent ion concentrations can promote more rapid gelation, but may also alter the final network structure and stability.

The evidence also shows that ionic crosslinking can be used to control gel properties such as insolubility, swelling, and mechanical strength. Ionotropic gelation is described as a promising crosslinking technique that can form water-insoluble gels under mild and eco-friendly conditions [N6-R4]. The evidence further states that the degree of crosslinking can be adjusted by tuning the ionic environment [N5-R2]. In the context of chitosan, this means that ionic crosslinking provides a way to tune gel properties while remaining environmentally mild and reversible in some cases [N6-R4][N5-R2].

## 4) Roles of crosslinkers and electrostatic interactions

### Crosslinkers provide covalent bonds that stabilize the gel network
Crosslinkers provide covalent bonds that stabilize the gel network. The evidence explicitly defines crosslinking as the formation of “intermolecular covalent bridges between the polymer chains” [N2-R4]. This is central to chemical gelation, where covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin create a three-dimensional spatial grid of chemical bonds [N2-F2]. The evidence also states that crosslinking can be used to form insoluble chitosan-based films and other materials with controlled sorption capacity and mechanical properties [N2-F2].

### Electrostatic interactions contribute to gelation via charge shielding or repulsion
Electrostatic interactions contribute to gelation by tuning charge state and promoting self-assembly. The review on physical gelation notes that electrostatic interactions are mainly ensured by physical/chemical features such as degree of acetylation and molecular weight, as well as external parameters such as pH and ionic strength [N1-F1]. The protonation/deprotonation evidence further explains that chitosan has a net positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) and is soluble in aqueous acidic media, while its protonation state can be tuned by pH [N4-F3]. This means that electrostatic interactions can either attract oppositely charged species or repel like charges, depending on the environmental conditions. The evidence also states that amino protonated chitosan can form a hydrogel with a metal complex anion through electrostatic interaction [N4-R5]. This directly supports the role of electrostatic interactions in gelation.

### Interplay between covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects
The interplay between covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects is important for gel morphology and stability. The review on physical gelation notes that both hydrophobic effects and hydrogen bonds govern gelation behavior, and that electrostatic interactions are a major factor [N1-F1]. The protonation/deprotonation evidence adds that the degree of deacetylation influences the balance between hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonding on chitosan [N4-F3]. This implies that electrostatic effects can modulate the overall conformation and interaction environment of the polymer, which in turn affects how covalent crosslinkers can stabilize the network.

Covalent crosslinkers provide the primary network structure and permanence, while electrostatic interactions can drive self-assembly and fine-tune the gel’s responsiveness to environmental changes [N2-R4][N1-F1][N4-F3]. The ionotropic/ionic gelation evidence further shows that electrostatic interactions can be exploited by multivalent ions, which can induce gelation through charge shielding or repulsion [N5-R2]. This supports the idea that covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects jointly determine gel morphology and stability.

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Physical and chemical gels of chitosan differ fundamentally in the nature of the bonds that form the network:
- **Physical gels** are formed by non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions. They are triggered by pH, temperature, and ionic strength, and they depend on conformational changes and self-assembly [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. They are less permanent, more reversible, and more sensitive to environmental changes than chemical gels [N1-F1].
- **Chemical gels** are formed by covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin, which create a stable, permanent network [N2-R4][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3].
- **Ionotropic/ionic gelation** is a special form of electrostatic-driven gelation, in which multivalent ions induce gelation through electrostatic attraction and charge shielding [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].
- **Crosslinkers** provide covalent bonds that stabilize the gel network [N2-R4].
- **Electrostatic interactions** contribute to gelation by tuning charge state, promoting self-assembly, and modulating sensitivity to environmental changes [N1-F1][N4-F3][N4-R5].

In short, chitosan gelation is shaped by both the **type of crosslinking mechanism** and the **environmental responsiveness** of the polymer. Chemical gelation is more permanent, while physical and ionotropic gels are more responsive and reversible. Crosslinkers stabilize the network through covalent bonds, while electrostatic interactions guide self-assembly and control the gel’s behavior under different conditions [N2-R4][N1-F1][N4-F3].

## Mini-report on chemical gelation of chitosan

Chemical gelation of chitosan is based on the formation of covalent crosslinks between polymer chains, which provides a more permanent and stable network than physical gelation. The cited evidence explicitly defines crosslinking as “intermolecular covalent bridges between the polymer chains” made by a crosslinker [N2-R4]. In the case of chitosan, common crosslinkers include glutaraldehyde and genipin, both of which are described as reagents that can be used to produce insoluble chitosan-based materials with controlled sorption and mechanical properties [N2-F2].

For glutaraldehyde, the evidence points to its use as a widely recognized crosslinker that forms covalent bonds with biomaterials containing amino groups, including chitosan [N3-R1]. The broader literature described in the same search result also notes that chitosan crosslinking can be carried out using a range of bifunctional reagents, including formaldehyde, toluene-2,4-diisocyanate, epichlorohydrine, and diglycidyl ether of ethylene glycol [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that dialdehyde crosslinkers are commonly used, especially glutaraldehyde [N2-F2].

Genipin is presented as a particularly attractive crosslinker because it is natural, less toxic, and improves swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of chitosan films [N2-F2]. The cited review further states that genipin reacts promptly with chitosan, as well as with proteins or amines in general, and produces blue-colored products [N3-R3]. The evidence also indicates that genipin crosslinking can be used to stabilize ECM scaffolds, including myocardial matrix hydrogel, decellularized spinal cord, or whole-liver scaffolds [N3-R5]. This suggests that genipin can provide a more controlled and reversible crosslinking behavior compared to some other reagents, but the evidence also notes that the reaction can be reversible and that polymerization of the crosslinker may reduce the number of molecules available for reaction with chitosan [N2-F2].

The evidence further indicates that crosslinker type strongly affects gelation speed, network density, and mechanical strength. The review explicitly states that “covalent or ionic type crosslinking reagents are used to form such grids of spatial bonds in films” [N2-F2]. It also notes that the ratio of functional groups in the chitosan–genipin system affects film absorption, sorption, physical, and mechanical properties [N2-F2]. Another source describes how the crosslinking agent can affect the swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of the films [N2-R2]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that different crosslinkers can alter the reaction mechanism and the final network architecture.

The impact of crosslinker concentration and reaction conditions is also evident in the evidence. The review notes that the degree of chitosan crosslinking can be estimated using experimental data on film swelling and water vapor sorption isotherms [N2-F2]. This implies that both concentration and reaction conditions can be tuned to control crosslinking density. The evidence also highlights that the amount of glutaraldehyde used can be important, because low but sufficient amounts do not increase cytotoxicity, whereas higher concentrations or other conditions may change the material’s behavior [N2-F2]. The cited review therefore supports the conclusion that crosslinker concentration and reaction conditions are central to controlling the network’s properties.

Overall, chemical gelation of chitosan relies on covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin, with glutaraldehyde forming strong covalent bonds and genipin offering a more biocompatible and reversible option [N3-R1][N2-F2][N3-R3]. Crosslinker type, concentration, and reaction conditions all influence gelation speed, network density, and mechanical strength, while the degree of crosslinking can be tuned experimentally [N2-F2][N2-R2].

# How physical and chemical gels of chitosan are formed, and what roles crosslinkers and electrostatic interactions play

Chitosan can form both physical and chemical gels, and the distinction between them lies in the nature of the bonds that hold the polymer network together. In **physical gels**, gelation is driven by non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions, whereas in **chemical gels**, covalent crosslinks are formed by crosslinkers. Electrostatic interactions also play a central role in **ionotropic/ionic gelation**, where multivalent counterions bind to the positively charged chitosan chains. Across these gelation modes, crosslinkers stabilize the network, while electrostatic effects tune charge state, self-assembly, and responsiveness to environmental conditions.

## 1) Physical gelation of chitosan

Physical gels of chitosan form when environmental conditions trigger conformational changes, self-assembly, and physical interactions rather than covalent crosslinking. The evidence says physical gelation is governed by hydrophobic effects and hydrogen bonds, and that electrostatic interactions are mainly ensured by physical/chemical features such as degree of acetylation and molecular weight, as well as external parameters such as pH and ionic strength [N1-F1]. This means physical gelation is highly responsive to the local environment.

### Triggers of physical gelation
The conditions that trigger physical gelation include:
- **pH**: Chitosan is a polycation under acidic conditions because its amino groups are protonated and carry a positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) [N4-F3].
- **Temperature**: Increasing temperature can speed up gelation, as shown by evidence that higher temperature can accelerate gelation and promote syneresis [N1-R1][N1-R2].
- **Ionic strength**: Ionic strength is an important external parameter that influences electrostatic interactions and thus physical gelation [N1-F1].

### Mechanism and drivers
The gelation mechanism is attributed to the formation of physical junctions, with hydrophobic interactions involving N-acetyl groups and hydrogen bonding playing a major role [N1-F1]. Another source states that hydrophobic interactions and reduced solubility are the main driving forces for chitosan gelation at high temperature in the presence of β-glycerophosphate [N1-R2]. This reflects how physical gelation is often driven by changes in solubility and intermolecular forces rather than chemical crosslinking.

### Role of conformational changes and self-assembly
Chitosan is amphiphilic because of the hydrophobic nature of acetylated units and the hydrophilic character of deacetylated units [N1-F1]. This amphiphilicity supports self-assembly and physical interactions. The degree of acetylation and molecular weight also influence the physical interactions that govern gelation [N1-F1]. In other words, the polymer’s chemical composition can shift the balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic behavior, thereby affecting gelation.

### How physical gels differ from chemical gels
Physical gels are generally **less permanent** than chemical gels, because they rely on non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions [N1-F1]. They are also more **reversible** and more **sensitive to environmental changes** such as pH, temperature, and ionic strength [N1-F1]. In contrast, chemical gels are more permanent because they rely on covalent crosslinks [N2-R4]. So, physical gels are responsive and can be tuned by external conditions, while chemical gels are more robust and stable.

## 2) Chemical gelation of chitosan

Chemical gelation of chitosan is based on the formation of **covalent crosslinks** between polymer chains, which provides a more permanent and stable network. The evidence explicitly defines crosslinking as the formation of “intermolecular covalent bridges between the polymer chains” [N2-R4]. In the context of chitosan, common crosslinkers include **glutaraldehyde** and **genipin**, both of which are used to produce insoluble chitosan-based materials with controlled sorption capacity and mechanical properties [N2-F2].

### Chemical reactions involved
Glutaraldehyde is described as a widely used crosslinker that forms covalent bonds with biomaterials containing amino groups, including chitosan [N3-R1]. The broader literature notes that chitosan crosslinking can be carried out using a range of bifunctional reagents, including formaldehyde, toluene-2,4-diisocyanate, epichlorohydrine, and diglycidyl ether of ethylene glycol [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that dialdehyde crosslinkers are commonly used, especially glutaraldehyde [N2-F2].

Genipin is presented as a particularly attractive crosslinker because it is natural, less toxic, and improves swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of chitosan films [N2-F2]. The evidence also states that genipin reacts promptly with chitosan, as well as with proteins or amines in general, and produces blue-colored products [N3-R3]. It can also be used to stabilize ECM scaffolds [N3-R5].

### Effects of crosslinker type
Crosslinker type strongly affects gelation speed, network density, and mechanical strength. The evidence notes that covalent or ionic type crosslinking reagents are used to form such grids of spatial bonds in films [N2-F2]. It also states that the ratio of functional groups in the chitosan–genipin system affects film absorption, sorption, physical, and mechanical properties [N2-F2]. Another source notes that crosslinking with genipin improves swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of the films [N2-R2]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that different crosslinkers can alter the reaction mechanism and the final network architecture.

### Impact of crosslinker concentration and reaction conditions
The evidence also indicates that crosslinker concentration and reaction conditions are central to controlling the network. The review notes that the degree of chitosan crosslinking can be estimated using experimental data on film swelling and water vapor sorption isotherms [N2-F2]. This implies that both concentration and reaction conditions can be tuned to control crosslinking density. The evidence also highlights that the amount of glutaraldehyde used can be important, because low but sufficient amounts do not increase cytotoxicity, whereas higher concentrations or other conditions may change the material’s behavior [N2-F2].

In summary, chemical gelation of chitosan relies on covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin [N3-R1][N2-F2][N3-R3]. Crosslinker type, concentration, and reaction conditions all influence gelation speed, network density, and mechanical strength, while the degree of crosslinking can be tuned experimentally [N2-F2][N2-R2].

## 3) Ionotropic/ionic gelation of chitosan

Ionotropic/ionic gelation of chitosan is based on the formation of gels through **electrostatic interactions** with multivalent counterions. The evidence states that ionotropic gelation is a phenomenon exploiting the ability of polyelectrolytes such as polysaccharides to react with oppositely charged molecules, such as cations [N6-R1]. It also notes that ionotropic gelation involves the spontaneous aggregation of chitosan with multivalent counter ions, most commonly sodium tripolyphosphate (TPP) [N6-R2].

### Mechanism: multivalent ions induce gelation through electrostatic interactions
The mechanism is electrostatic. Chitosan is a polycation under acidic conditions because its amino groups are protonated and carry a positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) [N4-F3]. Multivalent cations such as calcium, aluminum, or tripolyphosphate can bind to chitosan through electrostatic attraction, leading to charge shielding and self-assembly [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence also states that the presence of calcium ions in the chitosan solution during incubation had a great effect on the ability of a gel bead to bind chitosan [N6-R5]. This supports the idea that multivalent ions act as crosslinkers by forming multiple charge-mediated interactions with the positively charged chitosan chains.

### Effects of ion concentration and valency
Ion concentration and valency strongly affect gelation and network stability. The evidence notes that the presence of multivalent ions can be modulated via adjusting conditions [N5-R2]. It also explains that electrostatic interactions between chitosan and multivalent ionic crosslinkers depend on the molecular structure of the anion and can be tuned by changing the ionic environment [N5-R2]. Another source states that the ability of a gel bead to bind chitosan is greatly affected by the presence of calcium ions [N6-R5]. This indicates that higher multivalent ion concentrations can promote more rapid gelation, but may also alter the final network structure and stability.

### Relationship between ionic crosslinking and gel properties
The evidence also shows that ionic crosslinking can be used to control gel properties such as insolubility, swelling, and mechanical strength. Ionotropic gelation is described as a promising crosslinking technique that can form water-insoluble gels under mild and eco-friendly conditions [N6-R4]. The evidence further states that the degree of crosslinking can be adjusted by tuning the ionic environment [N5-R2]. In the context of chitosan, this means that ionic crosslinking provides a way to tune gel properties while remaining environmentally mild and reversible in some cases [N6-R4][N5-R2].

## 4) Roles of crosslinkers and electrostatic interactions

### Crosslinkers provide covalent bonds that stabilize the gel network
Crosslinkers provide covalent bonds that stabilize the gel network. The evidence explicitly defines crosslinking as the formation of “intermolecular covalent bridges between the polymer chains” [N2-R4]. This is central to chemical gelation, where covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin create a three-dimensional spatial grid of chemical bonds [N2-F2]. The evidence also states that crosslinking can be used to form insoluble chitosan-based films and other materials with controlled sorption capacity and mechanical properties [N2-F2].

### Electrostatic interactions contribute to gelation via charge shielding or repulsion
Electrostatic interactions contribute to gelation by tuning charge state and promoting self-assembly. The review on physical gelation notes that electrostatic interactions are mainly ensured by physical/chemical features such as degree of acetylation and molecular weight, as well as external parameters such as pH and ionic strength [N1-F1]. The protonation/deprotonation evidence further explains that chitosan has a net positive charge below its pKa (~6.2–6.5) and is soluble in aqueous acidic media, while its protonation state can be tuned by pH [N4-F3]. This means that electrostatic interactions can either attract oppositely charged species or repel like charges, depending on the environmental conditions. The evidence also states that amino protonated chitosan can form a hydrogel with a metal complex anion through electrostatic interaction [N4-R5]. This directly supports the role of electrostatic interactions in gelation.

### Interplay between covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects
The interplay between covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects is important for gel morphology and stability. The review on physical gelation notes that both hydrophobic effects and hydrogen bonds govern gelation behavior, and that electrostatic interactions are a major factor [N1-F1]. The protonation/deprotonation evidence adds that the degree of deacetylation influences the balance between hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonding on chitosan [N4-F3]. This implies that electrostatic effects can modulate the overall conformation and interaction environment of the polymer, which in turn affects how covalent crosslinkers can stabilize the network.

The evidence also suggests that covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects can have complementary roles. Covalent crosslinkers provide the primary network structure and permanence, while electrostatic interactions can drive self-assembly and fine-tune the gel’s responsiveness to environmental changes [N2-R4][N1-F1][N4-F3]. The ionotropic/ionic gelation evidence further shows that electrostatic interactions can be exploited by multivalent ions, which can induce gelation through charge shielding or repulsion [N5-R2]. This supports the idea that covalent crosslinking and electrostatic effects jointly determine gel morphology and stability.

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Physical and chemical gels of chitosan differ fundamentally in the nature of the bonds that form the network:
- **Physical gels** are formed by non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions. They are triggered by pH, temperature, and ionic strength, and they depend on conformational changes and self-assembly [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. They are less permanent, more reversible, and more sensitive to environmental changes than chemical gels [N1-F1].
- **Chemical gels** are formed by covalent crosslinkers such as glutaraldehyde and genipin, which create a stable, permanent network [N2-R4][N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3].
- **Ionotropic/ionic gelation** is a special form of electrostatic-driven gelation, in which multivalent ions induce gelation through electrostatic attraction and charge shielding [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].
- **Crosslinkers** provide covalent bonds that stabilize the gel network [N2-R4].
- **Electrostatic interactions** contribute to gelation by tuning charge state, promoting self-assembly, and modulating sensitivity to environmental changes [N1-F1][N4-F3][N4-R5].

In short, chitosan gelation is shaped by both the **type of crosslinking mechanism** and the **environmental responsiveness** of the polymer. Chemical gelation is more permanent, while physical and ionotropic gels are more responsive and reversible. Crosslinkers stabilize the network through covalent bonds, while electrostatic interactions guide self-assembly and control the gel’s behavior under different conditions [N2-R4][N1-F1][N4-F3].

The gelation mechanism is attributed to the formation of physical junctions, with hydrophobic interactions involving N-acetyl groups and hydrogen bonding playing a major role [N1-F1]. Physical gels are generally **less permanent** than chemical gels, because they rely on non-covalent interactions such as hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic interactions [N1-F1]. The broader literature notes that chitosan crosslinking can be carried out using a range of bifunctional reagents, including formaldehyde, toluene-2,4-diisocyanate, epichlorohydrine, and diglycidyl ether of ethylene glycol [N2-F2]. It also emphasizes that dialdehyde crosslinkers are commonly used, especially glutaraldehyde [N2-F2].

Genipin is presented as a particularly attractive crosslinker because it is natural, less toxic, and improves swelling, water resistance, and mechanical properties of chitosan films [N2-F2].
